utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We are continuing with examination-in-chief, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise to Mr. Pantelic, but if we could have some assistance from the technical booth. We are not receiving transcript on the laptops. None of these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think the technical booth will be informed. But since the monitors are working, we can proceed. Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Blagojevic. What is the situation with your baggage like? Have you recovered it.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has arrived. It arrived 15 minutes ago, so everything is okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yesterday we spoke about the situation with refugees and you said that -- you described how you had organised the work of your secretariat. In this connection, will you please comment on an exhibit which has already been tendered here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have exhibit, please, D118/1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Until this document is found, Mr. Blagojevic, would you briefly describe for us whether you cooperated with any other persons on the subject-matter of refugees from the fall of 1992 and on, and how did this function in practice?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The secretariat for housing and utilities affairs, landscaping and town planning actually cooperated with the civil defence, with the Red Cross organisations, also it helped carry out repair projects on damaged buildings, together with the Department of Defence sector, from which we were given the necessary labour force to repair such structures. And normally we also cooperated with the relevant departments, ministries, that is, the ministry for housing and utilities and landscaping of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Will you now look at this document which is to your right side. If it is easier for you, you can look at the document directly. You don't have to look at it on the screen, because on the screen you only have a part of it. Feel free to take the document, to take a closer look at the document and familiarise yourself with it. What can you say about this document?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was adopted towards the end of 1992. This commission was an operational body, in fact. Its task was to identify the most acute problems, for instance, when a larger group of refugees appeared, where to accommodate them, how to accommodate them, and the composition of this commission was such as to enable the commission to identify all the needs of this population segment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did the commission in this membership function for a long time or were there any changes in its membership?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We worked on an ad hoc basis, so whenever a major problem cropped up, we saw to address it by sitting in an adequate composition, and occasionally we would get some information, and I, as the chairman of this commission, would get information from other people who were, as a rule, the chairmen or the leaders of some other organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Can we now discuss another document?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have now Exhibit D131/1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can look to your right side again, at the document. You said that you had contacts with the Ministry of Defence department in Samac. In respect of certain people of given specialties which were supposed to help your secretariat in its work. So what is this document about and what was the reason for your establishing contacts with the -- this department of that ministry?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a period when the secretariat actually commenced its work, and it was my obligation to man -- actually, to request from the ministry two people, two people of the construction profession who were supposed to be assigned to work to repair structures and buildings. Mr. Rado Djurdjevic, a graduated architect, bachelor of architecture, worked in the secretariat, and also Djoko Bosic. He also worked in the secretariat. He worked on the accommodation of the needy population, population in need of accommodation. And Mr. Milan Babic worked, but only occasionally, with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I can see from this document that the people under numbers 1 and 2 were in a military unit, and also that they were obviously to be transferred, assigned to work within the framework of work duty. Would you please explain to me what this relationship was or how this relationship with the military units functioned, namely, if you needed to have men of specific skills, professional profile, engaged for the work of your secretariat.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the procedure: The secretariat, my secretariat, as well as others, as well as state-owned enterprises, would submit applications to the Ministry of Defence and the Ministry of Defence would contact military units, and it was within the competence of the military units to decide whether this was possible or whether the possibility existed for such a person to be assigned to work duty or not. If the military unit elected to go then they would receive decisions to that effect, decisions about the work obligation from the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. You also spoke about certain damage to the buildings due to war operations, although this is not directly associated with the period relevant to you, according to its date. Perhaps you can also comment on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pantelic. I really don't quite understand your question. When you're asking the witness about damaged buildings, but then you say: "Although this is not directly associated with the period relevant to you, according to its date." How will the witness be able to tell us anything if it isn't relevant to him, according to its date?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, this exhibit that I have in my list is D79/1, and since this witness testified yesterday that he -- when he assumed his position when he was assigned for the secretary of this department, he collected certain number of documents and the files in the office. So maybe he's aware about the activities of his department prior to his assignment, and also maybe he can give us some additional information how he conducted this kind of activity during his period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: As long as he knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And also as long as this is relevant to the indictment as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. Could we have Exhibit D79/1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tell me, in the meantime: Yesterday you said that your secretariat undertook certain activities to rectify it, to alleviate the consequences of the shelling in the Samac municipality. Did this refer to all the nationalities, to people of all ethnicities in Samac?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did. We repaired buildings, primarily housing units, residential houses, which were damaged and in which no conditions any longer existed for habitation, especially when it came to the actual town, a street called Vijenac, JNA Vijenac, which was along the Sava River, was very badly damaged and there lived a lot of Muslims. Once when the city came under -- when it was bombed by plane from Croatia, which bombed the waterworks and houses of the five severely damaged houses, three were Muslim houses, and we repaired those. Perhaps I could recall the names if that is essential in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do, if you can remember.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Arapovic. I believe that his first name was Nurija. Sebisic Anto, who was a Croat, and several other people whom I knew for a long time, but I cannot recollect their names at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Would you look at this document to your right. It has two pages. You can turn the leaves. Tell me something about this form of application for building material. Was this the practice of your secretariat? Was this the form it used, used by individuals in local communes to apply for such material, in practice?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have a rigidly defined application form. The regulation which was issued in June, prior to the work of our secretariat, in other words, by a man who worked as his work duty with the secretariat and who had worked for a very long time before that with the state enterprise for the management of housing, of the housing stock, he compiled the necessary data from the grounds and actually told us specifically what kind of material was required by what specific people in each particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me: In the procedure of work of your secretariat, had you ever had cases of forcibly evicting people who had no legal grounds or had no proper decisions, that had occupied the houses or flats of others on such a basis, without such a document?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, this was a very difficult but frequent job that the secretariat had to do, namely, as I said yesterday, people who were in a state of need would submit their applications for accommodation. However, many people submitted such applications without meeting the requirements for such accommodation to be allocated to them. So such people would occasionally forcibly enter some of the flats, or they would occupy inadequate flats for their needs, which were larger than they required, or houses, so that in order to maintain order and to allocate on an equitable basis what was available of the housing stock to us, we had to evict such people who had unlawfully taken occupancy. These were members of the army or civilians or people assigned to work duty. So that as a rule these were Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: With what services did you coordinate such activities? How was this procedure regulated legally and in accordance with the administrative procedure?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we received information from citizens or ex officio, with the assistance of the police, we evicted people who had unlawfully occupied houses or flats, and we would then return such houses or flats to the -- their original tenants or would later allocate them to individuals or families in need of accommodation for their use.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: In your practice, did you have cases of moving out unlawfully -- unlawful occupants of Serb ethnicity from apartments or houses that were owned by non-Serbs? Can you recollect any such cases?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the most frequent cases. I can remember the case of the Mitrovic family. That family was in need of accommodation, because earlier on they lived in the village of Brvnik, which was very badly damaged, and their own house was totally destroyed. However, in view of the fact that they lived in the countryside and that it was a typical farming family, we wanted to find accommodation for them in the countryside again, in an agricultural estate or farm. Or the example of a certain Mr. Pisarevic, who lived close to Samac, in the village of Pisari, and he unlawfully broke into an apartment. The policeman on duty, true enough, was informed by the citizens of this, or actually saw them, and we moved this person out because he had his own house which had not been damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let us make a correction in the transcript. [In English] Line 25. [Interpretation] You mentioned a location from which the Mitrovici family came. Could you give us the name? Could you pronounce it clearly for the transcript?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name of the village is Brvnik. B-R-V-N-I-K.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Regarding the cases that you have mentioned, whose apartments had they unlawfully moved into? Of what ethnicity were the citizens into whose apartments these people moved into unlawfully, the cases that you mentioned? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mitrovic moved into a house owned by a Croat, which was in the centre of town, and Mr. Pisarevic moved into an apartment of a certain Kapetanovic, therefore a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: After the normal proceedings were carried out, did the owners or the lawful tenants, the non-Serbs, did they regain control of occupancy of their apartments?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember the name of a lady, Jadranka Kapetanovic. Her apartment was restored to her, and she lived there for a while, in Samac. After that, she left Samac. As for the house that the Mitrovici had moved into had been abandoned, so the owners were not in is Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I wonder whether, Mr. Blagojevic, you could give us your view of what constituted abandoned property.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Abandoned property, according to the decree, was a property that the owners or occupants who had tenancy rights were not occupying, were not living in. This was defined according to the decree that they were not living there for more than 30 days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Did they have to have shown some type of intention not to return after the 30 days, or was it just 30 days and then it was abandoned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had no information about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: I have a question here. Do you have any knowledge of why there were so-called abandoned houses and apartments?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said yesterday that there were many families who had left Samac even before the outbreak of the war, the very beginning of the war. In view of the fact that war operations throughout Bosnia, including Samac, were very intensive, many people who had a chance to do so left the town and the municipality, not just Croats and Muslims, but also Serbs. And it was into those premises that we moved refugees into, and refugees were most numerous at least during 1992 from Gradacac, Zavidovici, Zenica, Kakanj, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: I have a follow-up question. Do you have any knowledge of where those people leaving the town of Bosanski Samac could find another accommodation somewhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Do you have any knowledge of where they went?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know in concrete terms about the people who fled as refugees to Yugoslavia. Among the refugees that went to Yugoslavia there were very many Serbs, but also quite a large number of Muslims as well. I think that the Croats were relatively few in number. Croats mostly went to Croatia, to stay with relatives or friends, and I heard that they also went on from there to Western Europe. There were also many people who were in Yugoslavia as refugees, both Serbs, Muslims, and Croats, who later also went to western Europe as refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you referred to a case of eviction. Perhaps you could comment briefly on this document that I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: D0022 and it's my intention to tender it into the evidence. By the way, there is also ERN number of the Prosecution office Y 0005296. So, Mr. Usher, could you just have this document to be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Could you, Mr. Pantelic, be so kind and repeat the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's D0022. It should be in the bundle of -- in the title of D00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Will you have a look at this document, please, Mr. Blagojevic. Have you any comments to make?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is clear from this document that the policeman on duty from the public security station in Samac found the people who were breaking into the apartment and changing the lock of somebody else's apartment, and eventually they agreed to give the key to the policeman, and then the policeman, the next day, returned, or rather, brought that key to the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Whose apartment was it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Mr. Kapetanovic's apartment and his wife Jadranka's.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Are those the people you were referring to a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have this document as an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The official note dated 21st of April, 1993, will be D148/1 and ter for the B/C/S. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The next document which I would like to discuss with this witness and to tender into evidence is RP 1. This is a decision to appoint the secretary of Bosanski Samac municipality secretariat for housing public utilities station, urban planning, dated 16 of September, 1992. Internal number is RP1.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the heading of this document, we see the legal basis for the appointment. Could you tell me what this means? Do you have any knowledge about the regulations relating to the state administration or, rather, the municipal administration, and how it functioned in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I see that the decision on my appointment as secretary of the department is stated here, but I do not know the legal basis. But I think it is the law on the state administration was the law on the basis of which I was appointed as secretary of the department for housing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So this is the decision on your appointment, whereupon you started working in the secretariat for housing and civil engineering; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But in the process of decision-making by municipal bodies, did your secretariat have the duty of preparing drafts of decisions that were then submitted for adoption? How did this work in practice?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As the secretary -- would offer to the Executive Board a decision regarding the allocation of a particular dwelling unit or some other premises to a certain person, and this would be drafted on the basis of a decree issued by the republic on the assignment for temporary use of housing and other premises. So that was the first document. And then on the basis of that document, there were other working documents that we would discuss at the Executive Board meeting, and after the discussion the document would be adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: During the work of your secretariat, up to the end of 1993, would you in the secretariat prepare draft decisions for municipal bodies: The Executive Council or the Assembly, relating to your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The secretariat would write a report on our work, and this report would contain the following components.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to that later, Mr. Blagojevic, but I'm just interested in regular daily decisions relating to your secretariat which needed to be adopted at meetings of the Executive Council or the Municipal Assembly. So did your secretariat draft decisions regarding housing, planning, public utilities, and things like that? Just explain that for me briefly, please.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Executive Council was actually the body to which our secretariat would submit drafts of certain documents, and through a regular procedure, once those documents were adopted, they would become operational and a basis for our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did anyone from your secretariat attend meetings of other municipal bodies as the rapporteur, when such a highly specialised document would be on the agenda for adoption, a document relating to the work of your secretariat?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My associates would attend, and so would I. Among the associates was Rado Djurdjevic, Djoko Bosic, Joka Vajagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, just reading the transcript, there's a little ambiguity in it, in one of the questions of Mr. Pantelic, preceding question. He asked if during meetings of other municipality bodies, when such a highly specialised document would be put on the agenda for adoption. Is he referring, is Mr. Pantelic referring to the document that is currently before the witness, referring to documents generally, or what? I get the impression that he's referring -- Mr. Pantelic is referring to the document that is before the witness regarding his appointment, but if I'm wrong, then perhaps that should be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure Mr. Pantelic will specify what he is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You heard the question put by the Prosecutor and the Trial Chamber, so could you explain to us now, please, what type of proposal, decision, so on and so forth, what type of documents were the proposals set forth, or rather where the condition was the presence of somebody from your own secretariat? Give us some examples, please. Describe to us how this took place. Give us several examples.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information as to the accommodation of these displaced persons was a frequent document that was discussed and later adopted by the Executive Board of the Samac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were there any other proposals or decisions?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. For the most part, this was information about the work of the secretariat. There weren't any other decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were there any documents relating to plan, town planning, municipal plans, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can we have a number for this document, Ms. Registrar, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The decision will be Exhibit D149/1 and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The other document that I would like to discuss with this witness is under the internal number RP2, and the document in question is decision on the assignment of residential and other space for temporary use adopted by the War Presidency on 17th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While I was just taking a look at this document, and you can have a look at it too. Leaf through it. It is several pages long. Turn to the last page, please, and stop there so that we can take a look at it. The date there, what date is it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is the 17th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now turn to the first page, please, and in the title, what is the date there?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 16th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So could you explain this to us? You are a man from the municipality. Tell us what all this is about. It's not essential, but let's just clarify this slight discrepancy, if you can.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume that the meeting was one of the wartime presidency that was held on the 16th of September, when the decision was adopted, whereas on the following day, most probably, which is to say on the 17th, the decision was actually written out, typed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, could you comment on this decision? I think you said a moment ago -- you mentioned it a moment ago. Could you explain it to us? What was the basis for this decision to be taken, how it functioned, and what you consider to be essential about this document.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that before my arrival to the municipality, before I came to it, the Executive Board or somebody from the Executive Board had prepared the text or what we would call a working document written down in draft form, for this decision that was later compiled on the basis of a provision at republican level, which was published in the Official Gazette in December 1992, which means that on the basis of this decision, the secretariat itself, which elaborated the decision in greater detail as to the assignment of residential and other space for temporary use to displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: May I have your comment on Article 2 of this decision, please. If you find it easier, you can take a look at the document on your right-hand side. What is Article 2, in fact? What is stated in Article 2? What does it define? But let me ask you something before we go on to that. I do apologise. Did I understand you to say correctly a moment ago that this decision of the 16th of September was prepared by your own secretariat as a proposal for adoption?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just studied it, together with the republican decision and provision, and it was actually prepared for adoption with certain corrections, just a few corrections on my part. That is to say, I aligned it, dovetailed it, with the republican decision, in actual fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we started commenting on Article 2. May we have your comments there, please.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The facilities that can be assigned for temporary use. It underlines here that they are always assigned for temporary use of persons -- or two persons who have need of accommodation, and for the most part these were displaced persons and refugees. So individuals of that category were able to be assigned accommodation on the territory of the Samac municipality pertaining to that article.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And next?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Persons who were assigned accommodation, what was the assigned, the facilities assigned were houses and flats that had been abandoned, that had been left empty, and where there were no other residents, as well as apartments that had not been abandoned but where there was extra space, extra living space, which could be occupied by these individuals. I think we said a little about that yesterday. So to sum up, this extra living space that the user of the apartment had, or the owner of the property had, if they were living on their own or had a small family and had extra space, having one or two extra rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: This decision, did it relate to the citizens of Samac whose own homes had been destroyed during the war? How did you resolve those problems, the problems of those people?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. All persons who needed accommodation, who needed a roof over their heads, of course most of these people were displaced persons and refugees, but also the local inhabitants too who had lost their own homes or whose living quarters had been damaged or destroyed due to the effects of the war. So those people were eligible too, and they were Samac citizens, and people from the surrounding villages which had also been destroyed and were either right up by the front line or houses that had been hit through artillery fire and damaged in that way, seriously damaged, of course. So persons of this kind were eligible for accommodation elsewhere. And there were quite a large number of persons in that category, in view of the fact that in 1992 the Samac municipality or, rather, the town of Samac itself, as well as the villages belonging to the Samac municipality, were in a very narrow encirclement. They were surrounded on all sides, in fact, because the front line was right the way around them. So that in all the villages of the Samac municipality, there were quite a large number of destroyed and damaged houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Blagojevic: The decision itself, did it favourise or did it make any difference in the ethnic sense of the people who tabled requests for accommodation? Was it biased in any way?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If you look at the number of inhabitants that were given accommodation, you would probably see that most of them were Serbs. But it was they who lived in the Samac municipality in the majority, although many other people who had come into the area and were non-Serbs were also put up and given accommodation, first of all in the town of Samac itself, and then elsewhere as well. But there was never any ethnic discrimination at all in this respect, both with regard to accommodation and with respect to the refurbishing of their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me a little more, please, about Article 5 and the following articles, the procedure that was used to assign accommodation to persons. May we have your comments? You elaborate that in the decision itself. So tell us more about it, please. Briefly, give us a summary of how this was translated into practice when you received a request for accommodation. What did you do?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When a request came in to us, we would study it in order to see who the person involved was, how large the family was, where it had come in from, where it was put up at the present time, whether they had any movables, movable property. And when I say that, I mean livestock, cattle of any kind, vehicles, tractors, et cetera. And so on the basis of all those elements, sometimes we would check them out if there was any indication of information being given that wasn't accurate and correct. So once we had studied a request that had come in to us, we would then assign accommodation in the presence of the individual being put up and we would draw up an extensive minutes about the state of the premises being allocated, the contents of the premises, as well as what was in the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you take a look at page 5 and look at Article 11 of this decision, and may we have your comments about that, please, how you applied the decision, how you put it into practice, this particular article.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We applied this article once we had accommodated the family from the territory and municipality in which the houses had been destroyed due to the war, and once their houses had been reconstructed and repaired, this was sometimes organised by the owner himself and sometimes by us, so in cases of that kind, when there was no longer need for these people to be accommodated elsewhere for temporary accommodation, we would return the families to their own homes. And the premises that were temporarily occupied, we would once again record the state of the premises in the minutes. We would list the property and furniture that is returned. We would align it with the first minutes when residency was taken up, see if everything tallied.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Point 1 of Article 11 is what I'm interested in. Could you comment on that, please.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When the premises are assigned, we drew attention and recorded this in the minutes to the fact that once the premises were left, the secretariat should be informed that the persons that had taken up temporary residence had indeed left, so that we could put up other people in the same place. This happened relatively frequently, because there was a lot of migration in the Samac municipality, so a lot of comings and goings. Refugees would come into Samac at one point, be accommodated there, and then they would move on, according to the dictates of their conscience. Once the conditions were ripe and they had somewhere else to go and stay, they would move on to other towns in Yugoslavia or Republika Srpska. Of course, sometimes when people left the premises, they would fail to report to us and tell us that they were leaving, and very often we didn't have -- they didn't leave any forwarding address of any kind, so we didn't know their whereabouts once they'd left.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the damages incurred during their residence? What procedure did you implement for paying for those damages?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the procedure for the most part was through the courts. We would take it to court. This was not something that my secretariat was in charge of. We did not undertake any proceedings along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have your comments to Article 16, please. Turn over the page. Look at Article 16 and give us some information about Article 16, to the best of your recollections and the practice that was applied. Because Article 16 was the operational article, was it not?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This particular article was very frequently activated, resorted to, because there were certain individuals who would unlawfully take up residence in homes. And what happened was that people who had accommodation elsewhere would take up residence somewhere, and they had perfectly good homes and houses that hadn't been destroyed at all. So these people wanted to have larger and better apartments and houses to live in, more comfortable ones. However, faced with the influx of more and more refugees and the increasing damage to homes and apartments in the municipality and the territory, we were forced to evict these persons who had taken up unlawful residence and who already had a home of their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Will you describe for us how this eviction procedure actually looked in practice of people who had unlawfully taken up residency? How did this function? Who did you cooperate with, and what was the practical procedure and the role of your secretariat in it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Upon learning that such a case had indeed occurred, we would invite the perpetrator of such an unlawful taking up of residency and talk to such people. As a rule, the result of most of such interviews was their eviction of such flats and of their own volition. But there were other cases when we had to also -- when we had to have workers of the public security station present in order for us to be able to evict people who had unlawfully taken up residency and had no right to such accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you have any information whether the procedure still remains the same today?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the procedure is like today.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can we have an exhibit number, please, for this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The decision will be Exhibit D150/1, and ter for B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The next document that I would like to discuss with this witness is our internal number D0020. It's a record of establishing, identifying, and assigning housing and other facilities for temporary use. This particular record -- yes. I don't see a date, but it's in 1992. Maybe this witness can help us with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Take a look, please. It is not a very good copy. You can indeed take it in your hand and familiarise yourself with it. Take a closer look at it, and then I'll ask you a few questions about it. Will you please tell us what this document is. I apologise. Before I ask you, before I put this question to you, there is no date in the heading, but I can see that in the beginning of the text that the date is actually the 1st of December, 1992, so that we can assume that the minutes were drawn on the 1st of December, can we?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Will you please comment on this document for me.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is indeed -- in fact a minutes on the establishment, identification -- and identification of houses being made available for temporary use, which was drawn up on the 1st of December, on the 1st of December, 1992, or 1993, rather. I apologise. At 9.30 hours. And then it goes on to list the members of the commission, Mrs. Mara Petkovic, civil engineering technician, Jelena --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the surname. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we have the surname of Jelena, please. The interpreters didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did you say the last name of Jelena, member of the commission, was?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vockic, Jelena. Vockic is the last name.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know that this happened in 1993? Because it seems to me that it was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue. If you find it easier, you can take it in your hand and take a closer look at it.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was in effect an inventory of all the effects of all the things in the flat. The former tenant which was Boris Mordjin. The document shows that this was a two-room apartment and lists most of the movables in the apartment, which were the property probably of Mr. Boris. We can also see from this document that Mrs. Lamija Hadzialijagic, with two members of her family, is accommodated in this flat. She otherwise used to live in the Vijenac JNA Street, which is the street which runs along the Sava River and which was exposed to constant shelling in 1992 and 1993, on the part of the Croats, from Croatia, rather. And on the 1st of December, Mrs. Lamija was left without any accommodation, so that we put her up in this free, abandoned flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what ethnicity is Mrs. Lamija?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Lamija Hadzialijagic is of Muslim ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me: On the basis of this minutes and the decision on the assignment of temporary living space, could Mrs. Lamija acquire any actual rights to that apartment as a tenant, in terms of the administrative and judicial procedure?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Lamija was accommodated in this apartment on a temporary basis, as the title of the document says, it is a minutes of temporary assignment of living space, of temporary accommodation. So that no other rights would be acquired by her except the right of temporary use, which she can exercise until the time when she has to leave the flat. So as this was the winter period, we waited for the repair of the -- her house, which then she would return to once the repairs had been carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you give me your professional assessment? Who was practically either the tenant, the holder of the tenancy rights to this apartment, or the owner of this apartment during the stay of Mrs. Lamija in it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The holder of the tenancy right to this apartment was Mr. Boris Mordjin. This apartment is on Pere Bosica Street, and the tenancy right, according to the regulations then in force in Bosnia and Herzegovina, i.e., also in Yugoslavia, in the socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, was such that practically over 98 per cent of all flats in the territory of the former Yugoslavia were either state-owned or socially owned property, and the tenants who occupied such flats were the users of the flats in question. A user of a flat was a person who was eligible, having met the necessary requirements for that status, and on the basis of a number of criteria which were set by the enterprise for the management of state-owned flats. Such persons would then enter into contracts for the use of such flats. So concretely, in this particular case, as well as in quite a few other cases, as I've already said, almost 98 per cent of the flats were state-owned. So in this case, Mr. Boris Mordjin was the actual holder to the tenancy right, not the owner of the flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Will you please tell me whether you have any personal knowledge of the actual structure of the ownership of real estate and houses and flats in the city of Samac, seeing that you held the post which you said. Because you just spoke illustratively enough about the situation in the former Yugoslavia which however is not of much relevance to this particular case. We are much more interested in the situation in the city of Samac. So can you tell us what the situation was in the city of Samac like?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, I suggest that this isn't going to assist you particularly to know the situation regarding property rights in Samac. The documents themselves that the Defence have produced don't purport to hand over or transfer property rights from these people who were supposedly occupying these houses pursuant to this decree and these arrangements that the witness has been speaking of, which he's already said that in this particular case, Mr. Mordjin would retain his property rights. So an analysis of the law relating to ownership of flats in Bosanski Samac isn't going to assist you much given that scenario, I submit. And I suggest that the topic is being exhausted by Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So maybe before you move on, though, I just would like to know whether the witness has any knowledge of the ethnicity of Mr. Mordjin, and also whether he has any knowledge as to whether the property was permanently or temporarily abandoned, and why, if he has the knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And with regard to the submission of my learned friend, I don't know. Should I repeat this question? Because I'm focused specifically on the Samac area. It might assist this Trial Chamber, since a lot of -- a great number of Prosecution witnesses testified with regard to the ownership of the apartments, of the houses, and maybe we could find out from this witness what the situation was in Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. As Mr. Di Fazio pointed out that we have the documents here which indicate how the property was being allocated to the people who were present in Samac, namely, the refugees, and on what basis, and how they were expected to look after that property. So that to discuss the actual law on ownership of property is not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just referring, Your Honour, to the factual situation in Samac, not with regard to the regulations, but in terms of numbers of percentage of the apartments in Samac. That's what I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I see. Because we have got sufficient evidence on how people were allocated temporary occupation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That appears to be a different topic. I've got no objection to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In terms of number, yes, statistically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. And also don't forget Judge Williams's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So please tell me: Do you have any personal knowledge about the situation in the city core of Samac? Because there were -- do you have an idea in terms of percentages how many flats were state owned, how many were those where people held tenancy rights? Do you have any records about that or do you have any recollections about it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Samac is a small town, and we had over 800 flats in Samac. The records were maintained by the state enterprise for the management of state-owned flats, which at the same time also collected the rent and the other charges paid by the tenants of those flats. And the records of this enterprise can actually also tell us which of these flats were in private hands. In Samac, actually, there were fewer than ten private flats. Most of these flats had been purchased immediately prior to the war, and they were in newly built blocks. Several flats were owned by private owners that had been built prior to the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what about the other flats? Would you please finish your statement.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The other remaining apartments were either state or socially-owned property, and these had practically been built after the Second World War, and they were constructed with money that had been collected in a specific way from state enterprises, which monies accrued into a fund which was administered by the enterprise, the state enterprise for the management of state-owned flats. They would provide such funds to people who were eligible for such construction, and this is the procedure which evolved throughout the duration of the former socialist Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And will you please now answer the question of the Honourable Judge Williams. Namely, do you have any personal information as to what ethnic group Mr. Boris Mordjin belongs, whose name features here as a titleholder to tenancy rights.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mordjin is a Croat. During the war he went to stay with his daughter in Belgrade, or actually, he went there for treatment. This is an elderly man. So he was ill. And during the war he went to Belgrade. And his daughter stated that he would not be returning to Samac as long as the war lasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: So the property would be considered temporarily abandoned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And a second question that I could ask you with relation to this document, on the second page of this report are personal belongings that were found in the apartment. And I would like to know, with reference to the previous decision, if Mrs. Lamija, upon leaving the apartment, would an inventory be made of the things contained in the apartment if things were damaged, whether this was recorded. Could you give us a concrete example from your own practice and that of your secretariat?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to the same rules regarding taking occupancy, the same would apply when people were moving out, and our practice was, for purely operational reasons, to adjust the moving in of a new family with the moving out of the previous family. So that was how we acted in practice. I can't remember this particular case. When Mrs. Lamija Hadzialijagic returned to her apartment or house, but I do know that she didn't stay there long, maybe until she moved out in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And who would specifically be responsible if any damage was done to the property contained in Mr. Mordjin's apartment?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, Mrs. Lamija. She was present when the apartment was assigned to her, and she would sign herself this inventory or report. We see another signature here. I think this was her mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You mean slightly to the right in relation to Mrs. Lamija's signature?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have a number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The record will be Exhibit D151/1, and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I have now another document under the internal number D0019. This is also a record, same as previous one, dated 3rd of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Pantelic. Before you get the into it, I just have one question for Mr. Blagojevic. Earlier on this afternoon, specifically on page 20, lines 19 and 20, in response to an early question by Mr. Pantelic concerning damages incurred during a residence, such as in the case of Mrs. Lamija Hadzialijagic, you had responded, on lines 19 and 20, by saying that the procedure for getting compensation was through the courts. And the quote from your testimony is: "We would take it to court." And I just want to be sure in my mind that what you are saying is that the administration, the municipality itself, would go to court to get compensation for the original tenant, that it wasn't up to the original tenant, such as Mr. Mordjin in D151/1, to go to court himself to get compensation for damage to either the real property or the personal, movable property. So I just want clarification that what I read on lines 19 and 20 of page 20 is correct, where you say: "We would take it to court."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Such complaints would be made by the damaged party, and I think this applies to this day. I don't know in which context I said that it was the secretariat who would take the matter to court. So it's the damaged party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Yes. In actual fact, you went on to say that it was not something that your secretariat was in charge of, but the translation certainly says before that: "We would take it to court," and that sounds as though it was a governmental function, and that's why I'm asking -- I was asking for that clarification. But now I understand that you are saying it was the person himself or herself who had the tenancy and what have you that had to personally go to court to get compensation. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We now have another document. It is similar in format, so we won't dwell on it for long. You've already explained some things in answer to -- in reference to the previous document, so please will you look at the second page of that document. Could you please tell me of what ethnicity was the person to whom this apartment was allocated, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is Mrs. Kata Tkalec, and she is a Croat. Tkalec, Kata. I'm afraid I don't know anything more about Mrs. Kata Tkalec.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could we have a number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D152/1 and ter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LINDHOLM
utterances.text: It's signed by temporary user Kata Ikosijac [phoen], at least in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. You're right. It's probably a mistake, because there is a question mark. Probably interpreters were not sure because of the bad copy, and the very -- the illegible writing, handwriting of this person in question. So I will clarify that for the record with the witness, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you please spell out the name, if you're quite certain of the name of this person, so that it can be part of the record.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it is Mrs. T-K-A-L-A-C. Tkalac, Kata. Kata is the first name, K-A-T-A.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, it's not Tkalac. It's T-K-A-L-E-C and then K-A-T-A. Thank you. It's the time for our break, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have in the meantime number maybe? Oh, we already have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We already have. We shall continue our break and continue at 1415.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. You continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Blagojevic, we left off before the break while we were speaking about the procedure applied in your secretariat, and you mentioned earlier on some other activities of your secretariat, such as the reconstruction of facilities, houses that had been damaged and destroyed during the shelling. Now, may I have your comments on the following document, please, if you're able to give them. That is to say, what it's about, when it came into being.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: D0026. The title of this document, it's B/C/S version one page and translation is three pages. The title is type and extent of damage to buildings. There is no date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Take a look at this document, please, on your right. Perhaps it hasn't appeared on the screen in its entirety. Tell us please, Mr. Blagojevic, what you know about the document, when it came into being, if you happen to know, why it was written, and so on, anything else of interest to us.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document which is a component part of the information given out and compiled for the assembly meeting that was held at the beginning of 1993, and in fact it provides detailed information about the damaged facilities in the town itself, residential buildings, industrial facilities, and the like, and the destruction and damage to facilities in the villages of the Samac municipality. The document includes the construction material needed to restore the damages, to make them habitable again, or in order to prevent further deterioration due to rain, snow, the effects of cold and damp, et cetera, the weather conditions. I assume that this is a document that was prepared for the assembly meeting that was held at the beginning of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The document is quite detailed, but I'm not quite clear as to the last figure, where it says "under miscellaneous." Is it 3 or the total number? What was the total number of facilities destroyed on the territory of Samac municipality? What was the total at the bottom?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this, it would appear that 1.400 facilities were damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the figure, please?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1.400 or 1.408, 1.408. But this information was received from the president of the municipal communities and local communities in the municipality, and the directors of state enterprises, as well as -- well, the document was compiled on those facts and figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What did you undertake in the secretariat to deal with the situation?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For most of the facilities, before we received information about their state, certain repair work was carried out, reconstruction and repair work. First of all, in residential buildings and industrial facilities, commercial buildings. A large number of these facilities were repaired by the owners themselves. We were not able to cater to such a large number of facilities that needed repair work done.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: As far as the construction material is concerned, what was the role of your secretariat and the municipal organs in that respect?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in order to repair the residential and other buildings and facilities, the secretariat had at its disposal construction material in two or three warehouses in Samac. It was mostly construction material that had been found in the warehouses belonging to the socialist owned enterprises when the war broke out, material that was already there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, if it's of assistance to Mr. Pantelic, the Prosecution takes no issue with the fact that there was reconstruction occurring in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We can have the document numbered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: We can just have the document numbered and perhaps move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Just one last question with regard to that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was the reconstruction conducted regardless of ethnic affiliation of the proprietors or was any distinction made, ethnically speaking, in the Samac municipality with respect to reconstruction?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was no distinction for residential buildings or anything else in the town. Whether people were waiting for their homes to be repaired to go back to them or for the others. And in Samac and the surrounding villages, there was a lack of residential premises, so we were forced to repair the buildings and homes as soon as possible to be able to accommodate the large number of refugees and other persons needing accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: D153/1 and ter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now I would like to discuss with the witness document D0027. This is a report on work of the municipal secretariat for housing dated -- well, there is no date, but it's obviously from September 1992 until the first session of the Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Blagojevic, what's this about?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is about -- actually, it's a report on the work of my secretariat. Similar reports were compiled previously, similar reports are compiled today. The problems here are much more difficult to resolve, of course, and comprise not such a large period. Previously, reports of this kind looked into one-year period. This is a shorter period of time. The document deals with a shorter period because of the dramatic situation that occurred in that period. And it enumerates what was done, it itemizes what was done. And mostly we would prepare a document of this kind several days before the assembly was due to meet, the Municipal Assembly I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. I can see on the basis of this report that there was quite a lot of activity related to residential blocks, apartment blocks, in the town itself. For example, this is contained on page 3 of this document. And I'm interested in hearing about point 7 on page 3, the repair of the roof on the Carrington building, as it was called. Can you tell us, please, whether you know the ethnic composition of the tenants of that particular building.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you the percentages, what the national composition was, but I do know for sure that there were Serbs and Muslims and Croats living in the building. And I knew most of those people very well. For example, the president of the Court lived there. She was a lady, a Muslim. And then there was a Croat living there who was president of the Executive Board before the war, and so on and so forth. So I knew most of those people. And we did repair the building. Actually, we repaired the roof, which was badly damaged, with -- because several shells fell on it, of great destructive power. And we covered the building with the same sort of material that was used on the original roof, a form of tin, and the tin is on the building now and is doing its work very well. I should also like to mention that the secretariat, whilst preparing the heating and water installations in all the private houses that had been abandoned, that were not being lived in and, and in enterprise that were not functioning, we engaged experts in the field to let out the water from the pipes and so on, and to see that even more damage was not done to the installations. I'm talking about the heating plant, which wasn't operational at the time. And we tried to implement the principles of good husbandry with the materials that we had at our disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, I'm interested in the period from September 1992 to 1993, in the Carrington building, was the ethnic composition of the tenants mixed?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me what the situation was like with regard to the ethnic composition that came under point 8. It was the building known as S28, the S28 building mentioned in point 8 of the document.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in the ethnic composition.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are -- actually, the building is right nearby the building I live in, and most of the tenants who lived there before the war live there today, and they were there throughout the war. There were Croats and Muslims, and they're there today too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, could you tell me about the ethnic composition in the S62 building, which is mentioned in point 10?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This building is one of the larger buildings in Samac, and it is referred to as S62, according to the classification that was applied. It had 62 apartments in it. The apartment block actually has a larger number of flats, I think 80. It is difficult for me to speak about the ethnic composition of its tenants, but like with the S28 building, the S62 building, which was much larger, was also -- it was considerably damaged in different parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Blagojevic: When the secretariat had to go on-site to acquaint itself with the situation, did you go too to see what the state of the buildings was like and what the apartments were like? And I'm talking about 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was my duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about you personally. Did you personally go out to have a look for yourself?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: My next question is: Were you able to see on these occasions which ethnic group the tenants belonged to? When you went to size up the apartments in 1992 and 1993, who the people living there? What ethnic group did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did see people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, who did you see?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the members of all ethnicities: Serbs, Muslims, and Croats. All of them were living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, under point 13 we see that there was some construction work done on the building that was called Lepa Brena building, the Lepa Brena building. What can you tell us about the ethnic composition of the tenants in that particular building?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, may I object to this line of questioning?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The summary that was provided to us by the Defence, as far as I can see, contains nothing that might remotely be related -- that might allow us to foresee this sort of evidence coming in. It's not here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: About the repairs?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What about point number 1, 2, 3, 4, problems of housing, reparation of houses?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And apartments destroyed during the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The shelling from the Croatian side, not the houses from the -- the shelling from the Croatian side. I thought it is covered by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. That might well be so, but this evidence is -- it's regarding the ethnic composition of the inhabitants of the buildings, the ethnic composition of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It is relevant to their case because of the persecution, inhumane treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sure. I've got no problem. I can understand it. But again, if Mr. Pantelic finishes in ten minutes and I have to stand up and cross-examine, we have got absolutely no chance of being able to check any of this information or examine it carefully, and so we're put at a disadvantage. The purpose of providing us with this summary is to ensure that that doesn't happen and that the evidence can be fully tested in cross-examination. Now, I've got no problem with extensive evidence being given of the damage that occurred and so on and what the witness did in terms of repairs of houses destroyed during shelling, but this is something else. This is the ethnic composition of people who lived in those places before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: -- and after. And so from that point of view, it puts us at a disadvantage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. I'm afraid, Mr. Di Fazio, I don't agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, you can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. On page 4 of this report, you refer to the repair of the house of a certain Mr. Tade Sebesic, if I'm reading correctly the first line. Can you tell me what ethnicity this person was?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Underneath it I see the name of Juka Arnautovic, and what was the ethnicity of that person?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Juka Arnautovic is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Under the name of Arnautovic, there is reference to the flat of Vlada Kolev. What ethnicity is Mr. Vlado Kolev.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a Bulgarian. Mr. Vlado Kolev is Bulgarian.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Within the group of -- where there are a number of names also features of name of Muharem Kapetanovic. Of what ethnicity is he?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Muharem Kapetanovic is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Within this group of people, do you recognise any other non-Serbs?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know Mr. Andjelko Lukic, about Andjelko Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Blagojevic: What other measures were then taken by the Municipal Assembly. You told me this has been prepared for the meeting of the Municipal Assembly. Do you know what happened in 1993 pursuant to this report and on the basis of your suggestions as the secretariat?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The secretariat continued practically to work on repairs and reconstructions of all these facilities which are identified in this document. However, the situation on the ground kept changing, so that some of the buildings were wholly destroyed by shelling which ensued, so that they were no longer to be classified among the category of facilities which could be repaired. So that we had a constant operation to identify the state of damage of the various buildings and to carry out repairs which activity of ours continued until the end of the war, although I did not -- I was in the secretariat until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have a number for this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D154/1, and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The next document which I would like to briefly discuss with the witness is our internal number D0018, dated 30th of September, 1992. It's a request for work force or labour force. I don't know. Sent to the municipal detachment of Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Blagojevic, please tell us briefly. This is also related to a situation which you described previously regarding work obligation and professionals. What can you tell us about this particular document?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a typical application that we would send to the division of the Ministry of Defence, and this has to do with a person who is of -- a builder by profession, a civil engineer by profession, and we knew he was experienced in organising of repairs and building of facilities. So we applied to the secretariat for them to assign Mr. Ramusovic to us -- to work with us as part of his work duty, to work within the secretariat, so that we would be able to discharge our task.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What is Mr. Ramusovic by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Naser Ramusovic is a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what his function was in this period while he was engaged within the framework of your secretariat?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ramusovic did not come to our secretariat. He remained with the waterworks, since the water supply enterprise and the sewage and drainage enterprise also had a lot of technical problems. So that he remained in that enterprise and did not work with us. That is why we reapplied and asked for some other people, for instance, Mr. Babic, who then occasionally worked for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have a number for this document, please, exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit D155/1, and ter for the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Blagojevic, you said that when you come to the secretariat, that you found quite a large number of applications there which had been directly sent before that to the Executive Board, and that of course with your people you tried to organise the operation of the secretariat and to address all these questions with time, if I remember correctly, this is more or less what you told us.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now I wish to discuss a number of documents with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... are under the internal number R24, divided with subsection A, B, C, and D. In fact, these are four documents, applications for temporary housing for various persons. Subsection 24A, R -- our internal number, the applicant is Ms. Sehapovic Mirjana, and the date of this application is 21st of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Mr. Pantelic, about this document, because it will be quite a lot of time going through one by one. Do they have a common denominator? Are they applications by persons of various ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Temporary accommodation? If you can classify them along those lines and then maybe, since the Prosecution have looked at them, we can move much faster.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, for your assistance. In fact, that was also my idea. These particular four documents, we don't need to go into particular details of each document, in order to save time. We could -- if there is no objection, admit them as, let's say, one exhibit, divided into four sections, whatever is practicable, according to the practice of the registrar. And of course, the line -- the position the Defence is to show that, for example, all these four documents are submitted by the non-Serb citizens, and this is the basis why we would like to discuss that with this witness. But nothing more. I'll try to be very brief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any issue by the Prosecution regarding these four documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maybe, Mr. Usher, we could have all these four documents in front of the witness, and then he will give his brief explanation. Then it will be admitted, in order to expedite procedures. I do apologise. Can I first have some comments from the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Blagojevic, before you -- I assume you have four documents; right? One of these documents relates to the application of Mrs. Mirjana Sehapovic; is that not right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... that's why I asked you about grouping.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Not to go into details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We accept the documents as they are. The Prosecution has no issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay.
