utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is not taking -- objecting issue with the contents of the documents. So simply go ahead and have them numbered.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Blagojevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It might be useful, so we're all clear about what part of the document we're looking at, to -- for them to be clearly designated with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Nor numbering yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Either by name --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. For numbering Mr. Pantelic can tell us this document is so-and-so. So we have a title, a description of the document by the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: By date, because they're four different dates. That might be a quick, easy way of doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. So Mr. Pantelic can go ahead with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Blagojevic, to expedite matters: When you look at these four applications, what can you say about the ethnicity of the applicants seeking accommodation from the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here we have three persons who are Muslims, the Muslim faith, and one person who is a Croat, of the Croat faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We're talking here about ethnicity, about their national affiliation, not about their faith.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. So these are documents which were submitted starting with the 27th of January up to the 18th of January, 1993. Excuse me. The 21st of July to the 18th of January, 1993. They are the same forms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me about the fate of these applications.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All these applications were granted. I know that Mr. Doric [phoen] continued to live in Samac, although I didn't know him from before. Sorry. I didn't know the other people from before.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter corrects herself.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... adequate numbers or how we shall proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. Can we have the number for the one dated -- the first one, the one dated 20th July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's R24B.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: If I may give the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And follow with the dates that they were submitted as A, B, C, D. That will make matters easier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. This will be Exhibit D156/1, and ters. The dated documented 21st of July, 1992 will be A; 20th of July, 1992 will be B; 18th of June, 1992 will be C; and 28th of July, 1994 will be D. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. All right. Next documents which I would also discuss with the witness are under our internal numbering D001, and it was divided in the subsequent 46, 46 documents, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, I have no objection to this document being tendered, but I can foresee problems, unless this is being carefully sorted in sequence so they can be clearly identified for the purposes of the transcript and for the exhibit. I know that registry has approached me and asked if the Prosecution has any view regarding this being given one exhibit number with subdivisions, and my position is no, I've got no problem with that. But how you designate the subdivisions within the one exhibit is -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Or maybe, Your Honour, in order to speed up things, maybe it could be appropriate to admit only one document. Because basically we are speaking about the same issue here. These are the refugees from the Odzak area, and then I can ask for the clarification and additional information from this witness, saying what is his knowledge about the number, et cetera, and that can be like an illustration of how the procedure was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I wouldn't be happy with that, if Your Honours please. We've got to be precise. We're not the only people who may be looking at this, and we've got to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. What I wanted to ask was whether it's from D0011 up to D00146.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. So these are documents discussing the same issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The same issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. So you can elicit the evidence on what the documents are discussing and then we will leave it to the assistant registrar to advise on how to have them numbered.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And if Your Honours please, just if I may add one more suggestion. Perhaps if Mr. Pantelic could read the ERN number at the top of each document. It has a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Do they all have ERN numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I have to withdraw that suggestion. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So we leave it with the way he has numbered them, D001, up to D00146. So you can elicit the evidence regarding these documents and then we'll leave it to the assistant registrar to number the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I have your assistance please, Mr. Usher. Could we have this bundle of exhibits D001 in front of the ... Just a moment, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Blagojevic, as you yourself can see, in fact during the preparations for your taking the witness stand, we discussed this matter. As you can see, this is a group of 46 applications for accommodation, submitted by different persons. You can place the whole batch in front of you and take a look at these documents, according to the numbers. I can see that the applicants come from different places: Novi Grad, Trnjak, Donja Dubica, mainly that area. And the applications were submitted in May 1992. Can you generally tell us what you know about these documents?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are individuals who remained without their homes, individuals from the area of the municipality of Odzak, the villages of Novi Grad, Dubica, Trnjak. I assume that the date placed on these documents is this very date, because that was the day when they were freed from captivity in Croatian prisons. In the progress report which we saw earlier, the report on work which we saw earlier, there is reference to the fact that 350 buildings had been either torn down, destroyed, or burnt down in Donja Dubica, so that we can say that the entire village and the village of Trnjak were wholly destroyed. Only some outbuildings remained undamaged in a number of cases. So that these were the people that we are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Blagojevic: Of what ethnicity are the applicants who submitted these applications?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The applications which I just looked at are by Serbs from these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me: What was the activity of your secretariat to address the problems of the applicants who submitted these applications? When you assumed the secretariatship in the secretariat in September, did you find there already a number of applications which were then subsequently repeated, and what can you tell me about that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The majority of these applications came in the middle of the year, as people -- and as people were being released from prison, they kept submitting these applications throughout 1992. We then accommodated these people in Samac, but after on-site inspections, if there were any conditions for them to be put up in their own homes or in some outhouses in their states, they would not be allocated accommodation. True enough, many of these people had to be close to the town or in the town of Samac itself, because they had very serious injuries inflicted during their time in prison, and they also were in a great deal of fear of returning to their own homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, a quick perusal of these documents, these 46 documents, indicate a large number were dated -- appear to be dated May, end of May 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And a few at the end I think might be June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: They all appear to be before this witness was appointed to his position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When he's off fighting on the front line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I wonder if there's any basis for his knowledge regarding the contents -- his giving evidence of the contents of the documents, how he knows of all of these issues, these matters, and so on. If there is some basis for him saying well, look, I can tell you about various matters contained in the document for various reasons, then I'll withdraw my objection, but at this stage there isn't a foundation for him to say: "Look, I can tell you what's in these documents for this reason."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I thought that he had found them when he joined the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. He may have found them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: He can explain maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That was the basis for my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Let the witness explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please explain what your personal knowledge is about these specific applications that you have been commenting on.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the secretariat started working, we received about 500 applications that had not been resolved. Among them were these applications that are before us now, most probably. I said that throughout 1992 we continued receiving applications from people from the area and that these applications were made at the time that they were released as they were released from Croatian prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Registrar, could we have the numbers, or how we shall proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be Exhibit D157/1, and it will be subdivided from 1 to 46. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Blagojevic, tell me, please: At the end of this examination, and in fact your testimony before this Trial Chamber, at least the questioning by the Defence counsel --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we have just a second to see which kind of topics I will clarify with this witness? Because I have some others which are not covered -- which are not of importance for the Defence case. Just a few seconds, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Blagojevic, your secretariat was accountable to whom in the hierarchy? Which was the body that you belonged to as a secretariat in the administration?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The secretariat for housing and communal affairs was actually accountable to the Executive Council, and my immediate superior was the president of the Executive Council or Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Blagojevic: Did you have occasion in the course of 1992, when you became appointed to that position, until the end of 1993, did you have any contact with Dr. Blagoje Simic? Did you have any kind of relationship with him?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did have contacts, mostly at meetings dealing with the subject-matter that my secretariat was responsible for.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me roughly, please: How frequently would you have contact with him during that period of time, from your appointment until the end of 1993?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't really be precise and give you an exact figure. We met less frequently when Mr. Simic based was in the city thermal plant. Mr. Blagoje Simic, I meant. I think that towards the end of 1992, Mr. Blagoje Simic moved to the municipality building and the office that was occupied before the war also by the president of the Municipal Assembly and from then on we would see each other more frequently, on a private basis and also at meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me: From the beginning of 1993, you mentioned that a local institution started functioning. You were preparing a report for the beginning of the work of that institution. What was that institution?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As towards the end of 1992 and the beginning of 1993, it was concluded that conditions were appropriate for the assembly to work regularly. A Municipal Assembly meeting was prepared and held in the village of Pisari, near Samac, and actually, from then on the assembly resumed regular work similar to what it did before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: Did you have occasion to attend meetings of the Municipal Assembly, as a secretary of the secretariat for housing and public utilities?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In that capacity, did you prepare certain conclusions or decisions or solutions for that assembly?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me: Did you cooperate with the Executive Council in the preparation of those proposals and decisions that were to be adopted by the assembly?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the normal, customary procedure before the war and after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please: In the contacts, official contacts that you had with Dr. Blagoje Simic, did Dr. Simic ever tell you to allocate a particular apartment or space to a particular ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Blagoje Simic never made any such requests, and the secretariat was completely independent in performing the duties for which it had been established.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did Dr. Simic ever ask you to evict a non-Serb from his house or apartment?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he never made such a request.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In contacts with you, did Dr. Simic ever demonstrate any discriminatory intent towards the non-Serb population in Samac, either by the words he used, by his gestures, or any statements that he may have made?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he did not make any such demonstrations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Finally, tell me, on the basis of your experience during that period of time, what are your personal impressions of Dr. Blagoje Simic?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have known Dr. Simic since 1991. In those days he was a young physician working in Samac in the health centre there. During the first multiparty elections in Samac, he was active in the election campaigns, and he was elected I think to the position of vice-president of the municipality at those multiparty elections. The president was a Croat. We had more contact as of September 1992, and it is my opinion that Dr. Blagoje Simic is a very decent person, and personally, I have a very high opinion of Mr. Blagoje.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... examination-in-chief of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. Before you sit down, I'm wondering whether -- actually, we are all wondering whether you have decided to do away with some documents. Your internal number is R29 and R32.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't think -- because R29 is related to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No, you don't have to explain. Just tell us whether you don't wish to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's Doboj region and the other document we only discussed with previous witness, Mr. Ninkovic. So my position is, in order to save time, to speed up proceedings, not to discuss these two documents with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So there are two.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: There are two. R29 and R32, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So we can return them to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Any other counsel wishes to ask this witness questions? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: None, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. Cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Blagojevic, you briefly touched upon your political past. You said that you had been a member of the League of Communists in earlier years but that between October 1991 and December 1993 you were not a member of any political party. Did you join any political party after December of 1993?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What party was that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the Serbian Democratic Party. I don't know whether this was exactly at the end of 1993 or the beginning of 1994, but I became a member of the Serbian Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And by that time, you had seen its policies at work in Bosanski Samac for a period of almost two years or thereabouts; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And having seen its policies at work in Bosanski Samac, you decided that it was the party for you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you were -- you said that you were the assistant commander, I believe, of the 1st Detachment, which was headquartered in Batkusa. That's a correct statement of your evidence, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And assistant commander, I -- is, I take it, a fairly high ranking within the 1st Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just -- I do apologise. With regard to 1st. Because it was 18th. 18th department. I just tried to clarify. In your question, for the moment mistake. Instead of 1st, it was 18th, but now it's corrected. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's a fairly high rank that you held in the 1st Detachment, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be one of the assistants is one of four or five members of the command staff, and for the level containing about 250 men. So that is the position I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And is it your position that the 1st Detachment, along with the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th Detachment, were local units of the JNA whose main job, or brief, was protection of the local population?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And on that basis, we had defence lines going from the village of Batkusa, Drvenik [phoen], and Brvnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And in order to carry out that task that you were charged with that you had, it would have been important for you, for you personally and for the command also of the 1st Detachment, to have a good knowledge of any troop movements in the area?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the part of the war that I spent on the front line was spent in position warfare. There were two separate lines on the one side there were the forces of the army of Republika Srpska, and on the other were the HVO forces. And only in certain parts of the front, especially in view of the season and the growth and lush vegetation, we would occasionally even see the opposing side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Certainly. I apologise. Perhaps I didn't make myself clear enough. I'm really talking about the period of time before the 16th of April. In the period of time leading up to that day, it would have been important --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I do have to object to this, because if I remember correctly, the witness stated that he was mobilised on 17th.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: In the 1st Detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That is the evidence of this witness, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You had no active involvement in the 1st Detachment prior to that date?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the command, but my duties were not -- did not consist of active involvement until the outbreak of the war itself. The command of the detachment didn't have an army behind it, nor weapons, and it was more in the nature of a reserve force.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Are you aware of the 4th Detachment operating in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Would you say that the 1st Detachment, broadly speaking, carried out the same sort of duties as the 4th Detachment, but in a different area?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 1st Detachment held the line at the village of Batkusa, Brvnik, and Grebnice, and to the left flank we had our neighbours, and there were units of the 4th Detachment there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm concentrating on the period of time before the 16th of April, before the 16th. Now, before the 16th, would you say that your -- sorry, that the duties of the 1st Detachment were, broadly speaking, the same as that of the 4th Detachment but for a different area?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the duties of the 4th Detachment were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So you were the assistant commander of the 1st Detachment, but you did nothing in the period of time leading up to the 16th. You did no training, you met with no commanders, you didn't discuss any policy, you weren't kept abreast of any developments within the military, you weren't told of developments within the 17th Tactical Group. Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... loaded question, because there are so many questions in this one that maybe should be asked one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it. I'll rephrase it. I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Is it your position that in the period of time leading up to the 16th of April as assistant commander you did absolutely nothing, carried out no duty, engaged in no activity on behalf of the 1st Detachment?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to the 16th and inclusive of the 16th of April, 1992, I was in a private business and was engaged in regular private activities, and I was engaged on the 17th of April, 1992. It is true that my wartime assignment was to the command of the 1st Detachment, and this is an assignment I received from the defence ministry, a legal body that provided wartime assignments to military conscripts. And that same principle was applied long before the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Would it have been, in your view, a matter of interest to the 1st Detachment if a group of paramilitaries arrived in Batkusa on a helicopter on or around the 11th of April, 1992? Would that have been of interest to the soldiers of the 1st Detachment?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, objection. First of all, we got the evidence from this witness that he was assigned in the 1st Detachment as of 17th of April, 1992. This question is related to the events allegedly occurred on 11th of April, 1992. It's a pure issue of speculation of this witness how would he be able to know what happened on that day? And all questions are related to his membership in 1st Detachment. All this line of questions. And suddenly it was shifted to the period of 11th of April. So I just know what the reason for this kind of questions are. Because it wasn't raised in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That surely is no bar, could never be a bar. Of course it wasn't raised in examination-in-chief. But anyway, if I may get back to the other aspect of Mr. Pantelic's objection. Firstly, it's stretching the bounds of reason to suggest that a man who is the assistant commander of the 1st Detachment has seen active duty for a period of months between April and August, I believe, wouldn't know of issues of concern to that military body. That is just -- that's just -- I don't want to mince my words. It's ridiculous. Secondly, the summary produced by the Defence indicate that this witness was a reserve officer of the JNA and a member of the 17th Tactical Group. Now, reserve officer, I think, means something different from a man who has been mobilised. Presumably, therefore, the only logical conclusion, it must be a reference to his being a reserve officer before the 16th of April. The question is highly relevant, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: There is no valid basis for the objection. You can carry on, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So simple question. In your view --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In connection with this question, I would like to draw attention to the fact that I think the question has been worded in such a way that it is not clear which paramilitaries and where they're coming from. So I think the witness should be asked whether he's aware of the arrival of paramilitaries coming from where, arriving in Batkusa, and then ask him whether that would be of interest to the 1st Detachment. The witness hasn't said that he knows anything about that event. So I think it would only be fair to ask the witness whether he has any knowledge about that incident and to tell him who -- ask him who those paramilitaries were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Would you just bear with me for one moment, if Your Honours please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No. If Your Honours please, I'm not asking him specifically about any specific incident at this stage. I may get on to that. But I'm asking -- it's perfectly legitimate for me to ask if such an event would be of interest to that particular military body.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. What I was about to ask -- to say was that the question is perfectly legitimate. The Prosecution is entitled to elicit evidence which may support their case, even if that evidence or the issues regarding that evidence were not raised in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So you can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So, if the arrival of a group of paramilitaries by helicopter in Batkusa prior to the 16th of April, would that be a matter that would be of concern and interest to the command of the 1st Detachment?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learnt that certain forces had arrived, but significantly later than the 17th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very well. I'll be frank with you so that you understand our case. The Prosecution says on the 11th of April or thereabouts, a group of paramilitaries arrived by helicopter in the area of Batkusa and that they stayed in the Bosanski Samac area for a period of months thereafter and engaged in military activities. Do you have any knowledge of any such group arriving? And the group included people who called named Lugar, Crni, Debeli, Pralja, other names like that.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I got to know them later on. I met Lugar and Crni, and I would see -- I think his nickname was Debeli, but I didn't have any contact with him, but I think I saw him around.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Now, have you got any quarrel with the assertion they arrived at Batkusa by helicopter in early April, around the 11th of April? If you have no knowledge of the matter, say so, but if you are aware of that, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I believe that the witness already answered that. He said that he learned about that much later, in his previous answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When did you learn about that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I learned about the arrival, their arrival, somewhere around the 25th, or perhaps the 30th of April. And during those days, I saw Lugar for the first time, or rather, that's when we -- that's when they told me this gentleman is Lugar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: By that stage, of course, you had taken up your duties with the 1st Detachment, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, within the composition of the 1st Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In your role as part of the command of the 1st Detachment, were you told of the arrival of these paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I learnt about it in a sort of informal chat about those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When you found out about it during this informal chat of the arrival of a group of paramilitaries, was it -- did it concern you that you, as part of the command of the 1st Detachment, had not known until much later in the month of the arrival?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, quite simply, I wasn't able to know about it because I did not take part in the work of the command, and so in that sense I wasn't able to conclude anything in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And of course it must go from your evidence, it must follow from your evidence that the arrival of paramilitaries in Batkusa was not a matter that was generally known in the community, or do you think that it was perhaps just you who didn't know about it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know exactly. I think that a lot of people did not know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you become familiar with the paramilitaries over the ensuing months, and their activities?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would see Lugar -- I saw Lugar towards the end of April, or perhaps the beginning of May, when the defence line in the village of Grebnice was broken through by the HVO. And at that time, he arrived with a unit, a certain number of men, in order, as we said, to regain the defence line.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The 17th Tactical Group underwent a change of name, did it not?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it became the 2nd Posava Brigade, that that was the change.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. And the paramilitaries operated within that military unit, they were part of the command, part of the structure of that unit, the 2nd Posavina Brigade, or Posava Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think they were a part of the command. I think that they were under the command of the 17th Tactical Group. Now, whether this was after they were renamed or after the 17th Tactical Group became known as the 2nd Posavina Brigade, I can't say. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll turn to another topic. In the period of time between April of 1992 and extending, say, halfway into 1993, did you have occasion to walk around, visit the town of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first months of the war, I went very rarely. I went into town rarely. That is to say, my command post was at Batkusa, and I spent most of my time up at the defence lines. I went into Samac -- for example, I went on one occasion when my business facility, which was on the banks of the River Sava, was seriously damaged by shells from mortars, and I attempted to close off the windows after the glass had been shattered, to prevent the building from deteriorating and to keep safe what was in the building. I had a flat there, so I would stay in my own flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. How far is Obudovac from Batkusa?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's about four to five kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Your command post was in Batkusa, and Obudovac is four to five kilometres away. Now, would you agree with me that the paramilitaries were headquartered at Obudovac?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You have no reason to disagree with that assertion, have you?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In the time that you were carrying out your duties in Batkusa at your command post, did you have occasion to go to Obudovac?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no need to go, and for the most part I didn't go. I didn't leave the seat of the command, as a general rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, I'm sorry. I've just forgotten the date of the occasion when you were wounded. Was it in August or at an earlier period of time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on the 17th of August, 1992, in Batkusa.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. And you spent about a month recovering and then you were appointed to your position in the department of housing?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How did you obtain the position?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that the people who appointed me to the position knew that I had spent most of my years of service in civil engineering firms and that I was in the managerial organs of the companies and whose instruction were the socially-owned flats. And the very fact that I had been wounded and that I was not able to work in any military -- on any military assignment was probably the reason for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. And Dr. Blagoje Simic essentially appointed you, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember whether it was the Executive Board or Blagoje Simic himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't want to waste time, but D149/1 is essentially your appointment document. It's dated the 16th of September and it's signed by the president of the War Presidency, Dr. Blagoje Simic.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Had you known him very well before the date of your appointment?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did know him before. I said a moment ago that I first met him when he came to town as a young doctor. We didn't socialise, that's true. But as Samac is a small place, we -- you get to know anybody new coming in with that educational background. And otherwise, Dr. Blagoje was born in a village near Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Were you given any forewarning of your appointment? Did someone come and discuss it with you, ask you whether you wanted this position, whether you thought yourself suitable for it, or perhaps inform you who was considering you for the position, give you any information about the appointment?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was the possibility of appointing me, and I learnt about this while I was on sick leave. I can't remember exactly whether that was the actual time that I was in hospital in Bijeljina or when I was recovering, rather, convalescing at home, or in the municipality itself, where, when I was free, I had my duties towards my unit and my other duties, whether that was when I learnt about it. Well, I accept it anyway, because I consider that I would be able to perform my duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You say you learnt about it while you were on sick leave. Was it Blagoje Simic who discussed it with you while you were on sick leave, or someone else, or you can't remember?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was someone else.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. By the time of your appointment in September, in September, the situation with the influx of refugees was such that there was considerable pressure on the municipality; is that your position? Pressure for housing, housing needs.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, before I get any further into this topic, this might be the appropriate moment for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take our second break for 20 minutes and resume at 1805 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. You can proceed. We shall stop ten minutes before 7.00, because there are some matters we want to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, the -- one of the documents that counsel showed to you earlier today, I believe, was D18/ter. I don't need to show it to you, because I think everyone will agree that it defines the sorts of buildings that can be used for temporary use of refugees and so on. And Article 2 of D18/2 refers to socially-owned buildings which are empty or abandoned, that that sort of building could have been used by the department of housing to accommodate refugees, couldn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And is it your position that you were pretty well desperate to find accommodation for these incoming refugees?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The situation was very difficult or desperate, as you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Would the high school gym or the primary school gym would have been useful for accommodating refugees who came into the town of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it was suited to that, because there weren't enough toilets and washrooms, and there was no possibility for preparing food, cooking food on the premises. So the refugees, the women, children, elderly people, sick people, there were all sorts, and it was much more feasible and more humane to accommodate people in the empty flats and houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: But I thought you just said that socially-owned property could have been used for accommodation and that the situation was desperate in 1992. Would there not have been a pressing need to use these large public areas, such as the high school gym or the primary school gym?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't want to -- I do apologise to my learned friend. I don't want to object in narrow sense. In fact, maybe it's a misleading question to this witness in terms of the notion what the meaning of socially-owned property? Maybe the understanding of my learned friend in such -- is rather different than the understanding of this witness. So maybe Mr. Di Fazio should be more specific when he used the word which is quite strange for the western civilisation, socially-owned. It might be a factory, it might be a building, it might be apartment, it might be a garage also, in our system. But therefore, I think it's a little bit misleading.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It sounds very broad to me, the description that Mr. Pantelic just gave of socially-owned property, but let's get some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Earlier on in the evidence the witness -- even apartments, some of the blocks were socially-owned, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Well, can the witness be shown D18/2, please. Anyway, while we're waiting for the document to be produced, one thing's for sure from your evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The high school gym and the primary school gym were not fit for human habitation because of the inadequacy of the facilities, such as toilets, cooking facilities, and so on. That's your position, unless I heard you wrong.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you know of anyone being kept at the high school gym or the primary school gym in September and October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think in September and October 1992 there was nobody in those halls, in the gyms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Have a look at D18/2. Article 2, please, if you could just briefly read that into the evidence and just the first paragraph of Article 2, which is -- defines the sort of buildings available for temporary use. Just the first paragraph of Article 2.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Facilities which can be assigned to temporary use of what belongs to social standards, catering facilities, residential apartments, flats, weekend houses, auxiliary premises, such as economic facilities, garages, sheds, and offices, socially-owned or privately-owned, or mixed property ownership if they are empty or abandoned."

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's not broad enough to cover a high school gym or a primary school gym?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That could have been used too. And in some places it probably was, where there were no other facilities. But as a rule, we used everything provided for in the provision.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So the high school gym and the primary school gym were empty in September and October of 1992, notwithstanding this pressure of refugees on the municipality?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: There's been evidence in this case, uncontested evidence, that there were many arrests of Serb and Croat men who were housed in the SUP building and the TO building and the primary school gym and the high school gym. Are you aware of that? Sorry. I'll clarify my question. Muslim and Croat men. I didn't mean to say Serb and Croat men. Numbering in the hundreds.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the period ranging from September, when I was in Samac myself, those prisoners, prisoners or detained Muslims and Croats, there were none at that time, in fact, or at least I didn't know about anything of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you know that hundreds of Serb and -- sorry, Croat and Muslim men had been arrested in the period of time leading up to September and detained in those places?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Such a process would have led to a lot of abandoned homes, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you avail yourself of the abandoned homes of -- sorry, the homes of people who had been arrested, use them for your purposes?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my knowledge and information, the people who had been detained and held in custody in the schools and gym halls when the secretariat began to work, there were none. They were mostly disbanded, released.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Accommodation had to be found for the refugees even before you started taking up your duties. Did you find out, in order to be able to carry out your duties, how that had been achieved? In other words, did you find out what system had been in place before September?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people were accommodated in the abandoned, empty houses and apartments on the basis of a list compiled and updated by the civil defence organs or the Red Cross. I don't know which exactly now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In which --

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I do apologise. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it was on the basis of those lists before I arrived that these people were put up. I don't think that they were put up in the apartments that were previously housed by tenants that had been detained, because their families, that is to say, the women, children, parents perhaps, stayed on in those apartments, so they weren't actually empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were you aware of large numbers of Muslim and Croat men and women leaving the municipality by way of a system of exchanges?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in what numbers. I do know that, however, people left the municipality in that way too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That would have led to a lot of empty houses as well, wouldn't it, that process?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And did you and your department make use of houses that had been emptied as a result of an exchange process?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people who were on the lists indeed were exchanged, because there were some who would come to the spot where we had agreed for an exchange to take place with the Croat or the Muslim side. But people returned to their homes. So for those houses or flats which were indeed abandoned, the owners which did not return, we did use them for accommodating displaced persons and refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So the Chamber can be satisfied that some of the houses that you used for accommodating refugees were houses which had been emptied as a result of the exchange process?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And as far as the prisoners were concerned, those who were in detention prior to September of 1992, you say that their homes would not have been emptied because their families would have remained there. A number of those prisoners would have seen their families depart by way of the exchange process prior to September of 1992, in which case the whole house would have become empty, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I guess so.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And the Chamber can be satisfied, then, that refugees were being -- some refugees were accommodated, placed, in homes whose inhabitants were either in detention or who had left through the exchange process, or a combination thereof?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I raise an objection to the question raised in this manner, in order to -- that the Chamber can be satisfied. I can -- I'm saying this because the Prosecutor cannot actually speculate what kind of a reply will be the kind of reply that the Chamber can be satisfied with, because there's no way that the witness can know this. Actually, this is not the way that this question can be formulated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. The objection is sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry. My apologies. Would you just give me a moment to confer and re-read the objection? Because I'm not quite sure I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The point is you should rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Is your evidence that a number of houses used for accommodating refugees had been emptied as a result of the exchange process and detention process?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I ask you to look at D150/1, please. This is -- you've seen this document this afternoon, and during the course of evidence you were asked by Her Honour Judge Williams about the notion of abandonment. Now, we know from D18/1 that an abandoned premises is one that's been left empty for 30 days. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did your department ever make any inquiries to see if a house had been left empty as a result of a person being detained in any of the detention facilities in Bosanski Samac? Did you ever scour the TO or the SUP or the high school gym or the primary school gym, or any other place, for that matter, to see if a person had been detained? Because that would affect whether or not the place was actually abandoned, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do object to this question. First of all, it's multi-barrelled, but it's not the main problem. This witness just gave very straight answer with regard to the person who allegedly had been detained, and he said previous, earlier today, on a question of the Prosecution, that the person who might be detained -- I mean, this case cannot be ascribed to the process of the work of his department, since the members of the family of such person are still in their apartment. So I think it was clarified enough. I don't know where we are going with this line of questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: He's given clear evidence that there were a number of people who were occupying houses that had been emptied as a result of both the detention process and the exchange process. It's very clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. That evidence is on record, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question, approach it from a different angle. Do you have any knowledge of their being a system in place prior to your taking up duties in September of 1992 to ascertain whether the apparently abandoned home might be the result of someone being in detention? Do you know if there was any system that existed, any system that you were told of?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of any such system.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was there any system after September, when you took up your duties, to check whether someone was in detention?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a rule, we collected data from the field, from the neighbours, and people who knew the owners. And on the basis of such data, we could conclude whether the person in question was outside Samac territory or in Samac territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Couldn't you have gone to Stevan Todorovic and asked him if someone was in custody? He's the chief of police. He might know who is in custody.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not go to see Stevan.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did it occur to you to go and see him?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we did not collect such data from those organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Is it your position that people kept abandoning their premises throughout 1992 and into 1993, and at least during the period of time that you were working in the ministry -- sorry, in the housing department?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: After you took up your duties in September of 1992, did people in Bosanski Samac continue to abandon, within the meaning of the decree and the decision of the War Presidency, did they continue to abandon their homes?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know what decision of the presidency you're referring to, but throughout the war, people, Croats and Muslims, left the war-ridden areas in various ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And did you take pains or did the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I would like clarify, page 76, line 16, when this witness mentioned Croats and Muslims, I think we heard some -- that he mentioned also the third ethnic groups, and it is not in the transcript. So I would like that to be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In your last answer you said that throughout the war Croats and Muslims left the war-ridden areas. Did you mean to include Serbs in that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That is in fact what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Now, let's get back to the issue that I was dealing with. The fact that you -- your department was using these houses to accommodate refugees was widely known in the community, in the municipality of Bosanski Samac? Abandoned houses, I mean.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. That was widely known throughout the area, and throughout the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, irrespective of under whose control certain premises were, the procedure, the way of operation, was more or less the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sure. So if a Croat or a Muslim wanted to leave the area of Bosanski Samac after September of 1992, they would have known that if they did that, someone is going to move into their house, because that's the legal system that's in place; right?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was such, and as I mentioned, it was more or less a similar or identical principle that was followed by all the organs in the -- throughout the area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, all the organs in charge of accommodation, that is, worked according to the same principle. During 1993 I learned from a certain lady who was secretary for housing and utilities in Zenica, I learned from her that they practically operated in the same way and that they encountered the same problems as we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. So essentially, all a Croat or Muslim who wanted to leave Bosanski Samac had to do was not abandon their property but come and tell you that they're leaving, and this process of recording of their property and furniture and so on could take place in a calm and unhurried way and thorough way?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And would you agree that many Muslims and Croats continued to abandon their houses throughout the rest of 1992 and well into 1993?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They abandoned -- that is to say, all the inhabitants of Samac municipality and of the general area abandoned their houses and flats, and I concretely know about the situation in Samac. I can name quite a few names, also including of Serbs and Croats and Muslims, and this is a generally known fact. They lived aware of the fact that their property, whether it was a socially-owned flat or a privately-owned flat, would be provisionally allocated to homeless people. Perhaps I could add here that people -- Croats, Muslims, and Serbs got in touch with the refugees, who had contacts with the refugees who were put up near the houses, and they themselves actually made -- agreed with such people for them to move into their houses. This had positive effects in practice, because that meant that the house in question, the property in question, would be better maintained, especially during the harsh winters, when houses without inhabitants would have meant more damage to the installations, et cetera. So the people who lived in those houses also undertook the necessary repairs of any damage that the houses had sustained, and in that way also helped maintain the house or apartment in question much better than had it been empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You were asked by the Bench regarding the meaning of abandonment, and you said that you didn't have any information about that. In order to be able to carry out this decree, to implement it, you had to know very carefully, very specifically, didn't you, what exactly abandonment was?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understood your question properly, but we did know with certainty which property had been abandoned, and all the property that was abandoned was not reoccupied the same day. Property that -- excuse me, that may have been moved into by a refugee, this didn't mean that it would always be occupied, because those refugees also left Samac and went in different directions. So such properties would again be allocated to other persons who needed accommodation or had an interest in moving in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was asking the neighbours the only system that you had in place for ascertaining abandonment?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that Samac is a rather small town, I think before the war the population was about 4.000 inhabitants, the town itself, so it wasn't really difficult to find out when we needed to accommodate a certain number of people, we would offer families accommodation, or several possibilities. And after a couple of days we would schedule a meeting so as to be able to establish whether the accommodation offered was really available for occupancy or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Simple question. Just tell us: Was asking the neighbours the only system that you had in place to ascertain if a premises had been abandoned? Yes or no. Or did you have some other system?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would call the owner to contact us in some way or another, and if he was present, then we could establish with him whether that owner or tenant was present. There were apartments or houses that appeared to be abandoned at first glance, but the whole family, or a part of the family, were staying with relatives or friends in Samac or the surroundings. And of course, such apartments were not allocated to others.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So you would make some sort of informal inquiry; is that the case? You might make a telephone call or ask the neighbours, but nothing more than that?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A telephone call was not customary, because throughout the area there was no electricity, or at least there was a shortage of electricity for the telephone exchanges to operate normally. But we would leave messages with their neighbours and acquaintances. And as I said, Samac is a relatively small town, so that we could more or less rely on the information we received as to whether the owner or tenant was within Samac territory or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you ever --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Di Fazio. I wonder whether Mr. Blagojevic, you could answer the question of the Prosecutor directly. He's asked you: Did you get the information from neighbours? And it seems to me that's what you're saying, but you're not saying it directly. I wonder, Mr. Di Fazio, could you ask the question again, and we could get a direct answer from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In order to ascertain if a premises was abandoned, did you first ascertain from the neighbours whether or not that place had been abandoned?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of the ways that I've already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did that usually satisfy your inquiries?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So you didn't usually have to take recourse to other methods of finding out if the place had been abandoned; just asked the neighbours?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't just ask the neighbours, but that too was a way of obtaining information.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who would decide to carry out follow-up inquiries, that is, if the neighbours hadn't given you sufficient information?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then we would make inquiries from family members, friends who were not neighbours but who were informed, or should have been informed, as to the whereabouts of certain people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you ever go to Mr. Tadic and ask to look at his exchange records and see if the person had been exchanged?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go to see Mr. Tadic, but occasionally --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But occasionally I would see lists or hold lists in my hands, listing the names of persons who had been exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did Mr. Tadic, in his role in the civil defence, ever come to you, try to give you lists so that you could have clear, accurate information of abandoned houses or houses that had been abandoned through exchanges, make it easier for accommodating the Serb refugees -- sorry, the refugees?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That would have been an excellent way of finding out if a place had been abandoned, wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It would have been a better system than simply asking the neighbours, wouldn't you agree?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would occasionally have these lists, and they were also a source of information allowing us to establish the state of occupancy of certain premises. But it was very rare for entire families to be exchanged, so that if we would see a name on the list and we didn't know whether he had tenancy rights or not, whether he had a house or not, whether he had family members who had stayed behind, so that this was not sufficient for our needs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Isn't it the case that most families would have wanted to be exchanged at the same time?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, then, how can you say that it was rare for entire families to be exchanged? Or is it the case that families were split up through the exchange process?

utterances.speaker: VESELIN BLAGOJEVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I do know that there was a process of uniting of families, but as to the methods and procedures in that area, these are something I'm not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, I'm not going to finish tonight, so this might be as good a time to release the witness and deal with that other issue that you wanted dealt with. I can indicate that I won't be terribly much longer with the witness tomorrow morning -- well, tomorrow, I should say, tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The witness will continue to give evidence tomorrow, but for now, he may be led out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber was informed that the Prosecution wanted to raise a motion already.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I have an oral application to seek leave to file a brief written reply to the joint Defence response to the Prosecution motion to exclude the proposed Defence expert evidence of Mrs. Leposava Kron, Ph.D., which we received today. The reason for the application is now that the Defence has made clear in the response the reasons why it wishes to lead the evidence from Dr. Kron, which were not at all clear from the original motion, which merely attached her report to it, there are several matters which, in my submission, require response from the Prosecution. They're only brief matters. It's several pages, and I'd simply ask leave to file a written reply by midday tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber will grant the motion and expects the Prosecution to file the reply as indicated by midday tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That was the only issue I wished to raise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber was informed that courtroom 1 will not be used tomorrow because the proceedings there are cancelled, and the Trial Chamber was desirous of our using the courtroom so that we could sit in the morning and afternoon, starting at 0930 hours. But some matters have been brought to the attention of the Trial Chamber by the Defence, so I wonder whether that is still on, whether there is anything against the sitting 0930 hours to 1300 hours and then 1430 to 1630 tomorrow, using courtroom 1, which will be empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we learnt, unofficially, from the witness and victims unit that the Trial Chamber intends to sit tomorrow throughout the day, and I had contact with my client, and he informed me, as I had informed the Trial Chamber last week regarding his leg injury, he was examined by the physician yesterday, and the doctor told him that he should use crutches for another week, and for six weeks, another six weeks, he shouldn't be exposed to any additional strain. And when I told him that we might be sitting all day, he told me that he couldn't be in the courtroom all day, and he would particularly be uncomfortable during the long hour and a half lunch break. I wish to underline that Miroslav Tadic would really like to attend the hearings, but according to what he has just said, because of the pain he has in his leg, he would not be able to sit for longer hours. I must also add that our opening statement should start tomorrow, and one of our key witnesses should be called, and in that case, Miroslav Tadic could not waive his right to be present. Therefore, our request would be that we work for half a day tomorrow again. Of course, we don't mind if it should be in courtroom 1. And I understand that Defence counsel for Mr. Zaric has a similar remark to make in view of their client's condition of health.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. It is similar, but actually not the same situation. During this afternoon, Mr. Pisarevic and I were informed by Mr. Zaric that Mr. Zaric has a scheduled medical examination for tomorrow morning. It is actually something to do with his eyes, and the specialist, the ophthalmologist is coming to visit him. And bearing in mind that this is a kind of doctor that doesn't come very often in the Detention Unit, he would like to use the opportunity to be checked, because recently he has a lot of problems with his eyes. But anyway, when we spoke with Mr. Zaric, he said that he will give his consent to continue proceedings in his absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think after looking at the problems, especially the medical condition of Mr. Tadic, whose case is likely to begin tomorrow, we will just revert to our previous schedule, where we shall start at 1415 hours. I'm not sure whether we shall retain this courtroom or go in courtroom number 1. I think that will be sorted out. Yes, we will be in courtroom number 1, starting at 1415. But we will have to stop at 1750 tomorrow, and then Thursday and Friday it will be the normal schedule. We'll adjourn now and continue our proceedings tomorrow at 1415.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 15th day of January 2003, at 2.15 p.m.
